warmup.q: A service's GC log shows young pauses ending at a flat 300 MB for days, yet its container keeps growing until the kernel kills it. Where should you look first?
options: A heap dump: the leak must be in the heap
Memory outside the heap: direct buffers, threads, metaspace, with Native Memory Tracking
warmup.why: A flat floor after young pauses means the live heap isn't growing, so a heap dump will look normal. The growth is outside the heap, where Native Memory Tracking, the direct buffer pool and the thread count can show it. The young generation size and the pause goal change how the heap is collected, not what grows beside it.

opening:
Back in the warehouse, the floor keeps filling, and the cleaning crew isn't to blame. It throws out every box that no note leads to, exactly as it should. The trouble is a list pinned to the noticeboard by the door, which someone started months ago and never stopped writing. Every shelf number on that list is a box the crew must keep. Nobody needs those boxes. Somebody still holds a note to them.

That's a memory leak in Java, and it surprises anyone who learned the word in C, a language with no garbage collector, where a leak is memory nobody can reach any more. The last lesson showed the symptoms: a floor that rises in the GC log, or a container that grows until the kernel ends it. The easy trap is to reach for a heap dump every time. A heap dump photographs the floor, and it can't see the yard out back.

In this lesson, we'll make the thumbnail service leak, count what piles up, photograph the floor to find the list, then measure the yard and give memory out there a return date. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a list on the noticeboard that nobody stopped writing. A histogram counted its boxes, a heap dump and its dominator tree found the list, NMT took stock of the yard, and an arena handed yard space back at a closing brace. That ends this track, from the first box on the floor to the last crate out back.

Now search your own code for a static map or a cache with no maximum size, and for ByteBuffer.allocateDirect. For each one, ask what removes the entry, and when.

Next, we'll leave memory for time. A program gets faster while it runs, without a line changing. What does the JVM do to your code after it starts?

sections.h: A box nobody needs, still on a note: what a Java leak is
sections.html:
The garbage collector, the JVM's cleaning crew, frees every object on the heap (the memory where objects live) that it can't reach from a GC root. (A GC root is a starting point it trusts: a local variable on a thread's stack, one of the workers' desks, or a static field, the noticeboard by the door.) So in Java, a leak is memory that stays reachable from a root after the program is done with it. The collector is doing its job. Your code still holds the reference.

Here's the classic one, a thumbnail cache with no limit. It's a static map from an upload id to its thumbnail, so the service can send the same picture again without redoing the work:

Java
static final Map<String, CachedThumbnail> THUMBNAILS = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // never evicted

static void handle(String uploadId) {
    THUMBNAILS.computeIfAbsent(uploadId,
            id -> new CachedThumbnail(id, System.currentTimeMillis(), FORMATS.get(0), new byte[2_048]));
}
Kotlin
private val THUMBNAILS = ConcurrentHashMap<String, KCachedThumbnail>()          // never evicted

private fun handle(uploadId: String) {
    THUMBNAILS.computeIfAbsent(uploadId) { id ->
        KCachedThumbnail(id, System.currentTimeMillis(), FORMATS[0], ByteArray(2_048))
    }
}

FORMATS is a static list of the picture formats the site accepts, and each thumbnail points at one of its strings; that will matter in the next section. Every upload adds an entry, and nothing ever removes one. Lesson 6 showed what that looks like in a GC log: the after-values of young pauses rise pass after pass, full GCs (collections of the whole heap) free less and less, and in the end the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError or spends its time in Pause Full.

The same shape turns up in four places, over and over:

  • maps and caches with no limit and no expiry;
  • ThreadLocal values, a separate value per thread, set on the threads of a thread pool and never removed, so each pool thread keeps its last value forever (the threads track showed one);
  • listeners, objects registered to be called back when something happens, that nobody unregisters (lesson 3's weak registry is one fix);
  • class loaders, the parts of the JVM that load a program's classes, that can't be unloaded, which shows up as growth in metaspace, the back room where class plans live, and as collections with the cause Metadata GC Threshold.

The first tool is a class histogram: a count of live objects, and their bytes, for every class. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram prints one after a full GC, so it counts only reachable objects. (jcmd is the JDK's tool for sending commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is its process id.) For the cache above, after 20,000 uploads on JDK 25, the top four rows were:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
   1:         52891       43157184  [B (java.base@25.0.5.0.3)
   2:         32777         786648  java.lang.String (java.base@25.0.5.0.3)
   3:         22654         724928  java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap$Node (java.base@25.0.5.0.3)
   4:         20000         640000  workbench.memory.l07.LeakDemo$CachedThumbnail

[B means byte[]. Exactly 20,000 thumbnails of 32 bytes each are alive, 20,000 more than anyone meant to keep. That's the clue. The histogram tells you what fills the floor. It can't tell you who holds it.

try.title: Leak, count, dump
steps: Read LeakDemo. Its first child JVM handles 20,000 uploads with the cache above, prints the top of the class histogram, writes a heap dump, and measures what the cache keeps alive. Its second child has -Xmx64m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and handles uploads until the heap is full.
Predict: which class tops the histogram, and how many CachedThumbnail objects are alive?

sections.h: A photo of every shelf: heap dumps, retained size and the dominator tree
sections.html:
A heap dump is a file with every object on the heap and every reference between them, in a format called HPROF. It's a photograph of every shelf, taken for a detective. You can take one three ways:

  • jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof from a running JVM. Its help text says "Impact: High": it runs a full GC first (unless you pass -all) and stops the JVM while it writes. -gz compresses the file, and on JDK 25 -parallel sets how many threads write it.
  • -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError with -XX:HeapDumpPath=..., so the JVM writes one the moment it runs out of heap. It's off by default. It's a manageable flag, so jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true turns it on in a running JVM.
  • HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap(path, true) from code, which is what the demo does.

You read the photograph with a tool such as Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer), a free program from the Eclipse project. It shows two sizes for every object. The shallow size is the object's own bytes: lesson 1's header plus fields. The retained size is everything that would be freed if that one object were gone: the object itself plus everything reachable only through it.

You can work out a retained size by hand on a small graph, and doing it once makes MAT's numbers obvious. Look at the figure. The noticeboard's static field holds the map. The map holds a table, the table holds 20,000 nodes, and each node holds a key and a thumbnail with its 2 KB of pixels. Every path from a root to those pixels goes through the map, so the map dominates them, and they're in its retained set. Add it up: 20,000 pixel arrays at 2,064 bytes, keys at 80, thumbnails at 32 and nodes at 32, plus the 128 KB table. That's about 44 MB, held by a 64-byte object.

The shared "image/jpeg" string is different. The FORMATS list, another static field, reaches it too, so dropping the map wouldn't free it. It isn't in the map's retained set.

Is the arithmetic right? Let's not take my word for it. The demo measures the live heap after a full GC, clears the map, and measures again. On JDK 25 it printed:

live heap 47,259,896 bytes with the cache full, 2,763,024 after clear(): it kept 44,496,872 bytes alive

That's 44.5 MB, the retained set we added up, give or take a little noise. (clear() keeps the map's table, which the hand count included.)

MAT's dominator tree lists objects by retained size, biggest first. For this dump, the map should sit at the top with about 44 MB, and its path to a GC root should name the static field THUMBNAILS. (I couldn't run MAT for this course, so that's what the definition and the measurement predict, not a screenshot.) A histogram says what fills the floor. The dominator tree says who holds it. Fix the holder.

Here the photograph picture breaks. A photo shows one moment, while a leak is a habit: the code adds a note on every upload. You find the list in the dump, but you fix it in the code that keeps writing it.

And a photograph of the floor can't show what isn't on the floor.

try.title: Find the holder in Eclipse MAT

Before you click anything, predict the top entry of the dominator tree and its retained size, from the figure and the demo's last line.
Open the dominator tree. Then, on the biggest entry, use "Path to GC Roots" to find the field that holds it.
try.expect: From the definition and the measurement, the ConcurrentHashMap should top the dominator tree with a retained size of about 44 MB, almost all of it in 2 KB byte[] pixel arrays. If your top entry is something else, compare its retained size with the histogram's byte counts and follow its path to the root the same way.

sections.h: The yard out back: Native Memory Tracking finds growth outside the heap
sections.html:
Sometimes the heap is fine and the process still grows. The GC log shows a flat floor, a heap dump shows nothing odd, and the container still gets killed. The memory is outside the heap, in the yard out back that the floor plan doesn't show.

Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's own inventory of the memory it uses, the yard included. It's off by default. Start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then ask the running process:

jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB

In the demo, a JDK 25 process with a 256 MB heap had committed 295 MB at startup (committed means the operating system has really handed it over). Then it allocated one 64 MiB direct buffer, memory outside the heap that ByteBuffer.allocateDirect asks for, and started 100 threads. Now it had committed 370 MB. NMT shows where the difference went. A category called Other appeared with 64 MB, the direct buffer. Thread went from 1 MB to 11 MB committed, with 120 MB reserved (addresses set aside, not yet used), because each new thread reserves about 1 MB for its stack but touches only a little of it.

For a slow leak, take a baseline and compare later:

jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB

The diff marks every change. After 100 direct buffers of 1 MiB, JDK 25 printed:

-                     Other (reserved=100MB +100MB, committed=100MB +100MB)
                            (malloc=100MB +100MB #102 +100)

A growing Other points at direct buffers or native code, a growing Thread at threads that are started and never stopped, and a growing Class or Metaspace at class loaders.

Direct buffers deserve one more level of detail. ByteBuffer.allocateDirect creates a small object on the heap that owns the native memory. When the GC collects that small object, a cleaner frees the memory, the same idea as lesson 3's Cleaner. In the warehouse, each crate in the yard has a tag on the floor, and the crate goes only when the crew throws out its tag. So native memory waits for a collection, and a big, quiet heap may not collect for a long time.

Unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, the limit for all of it is the max heap size. Set it, and a direct-buffer leak fails loudly instead of quietly, with a stack trace that points at the code:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 67108864 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 33554432)

A crate that leaves only when the crew passes by is awkward, though. Sometimes you know exactly when you're done with it.

try.title: Watch native memory move
steps: Read NmtDemo. Its first child runs with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and prints NMT's summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 threads. Its second child asks for 64 MiB of direct memory under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m.
Predict which NMT categories change, and by how much. Then run it.

code.title: NmtDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l07; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import javax.management.ObjectName; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Native Memory Tracking from inside a child JVM: the summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer * and 100 extra threads. Then a direct buffer that doesn't fit under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize. */ public class NmtDemo { static final Pattern CATEGORY = Pattern.compile("^-?\\s*(Total|[A-Z][\\w ]+?):? \\(?reserved=(\\d+)MB, committed=(\\d+)MB"); static String nativeMemory() throws Exception { // the same as: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB return (String) ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( new ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", new Object[] {new String[] {"summary", "scale=MB"}}, new String[] {String[].class.getName()}); } static void print(String title) throws Exception { System.out.println(title); for (String line : nativeMemory().lines().toList()) { Matcher m = CATEGORY.matcher(line); if (m.find()) System.out.printf(" %-20s committed %,5d MB (reserved %,5d MB)%n", m.group(1), Long.parseLong(m.group(3)), Long.parseLong(m.group(2))); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length == 0) { Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"), NmtDemo.class.getName(), "track"); Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m"), NmtDemo.class.getName(), "limit"); return; } if (args[0].equals("limit")) { try { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024); } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) { System.out.println("with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m: " + e); } return; } print("at startup"); ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024); // network code often keeps socket data in these CountDownLatch never = new CountDownLatch(1); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { never.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } }); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } print("after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 more threads"); System.out.println("buffer " + direct.capacity()); } }

sections.h: Off-heap memory with a return date: arenas in the FFM API
sections.html:
The Foreign Function and Memory API (FFM), final since JDK 22 (JEP 454), gives memory outside the heap a lifetime you control. Memory comes from an arena, and the arena decides when that memory is freed. In the warehouse, an arena is a corner of the yard rented with a return date, handed back all at once.

Arena Lifetime Closed by Threads
Arena.global() until the JVM exits nobody any
Arena.ofAuto() until the GC finds it unreachable the GC any
Arena.ofConfined() until you call close() you, from the owner thread the owner only
Arena.ofShared() until you call close() you, from any thread any

A confined arena in try-with-resources frees its memory at the closing brace. No GC is involved, so there's nothing to wait for. A memory segment is the block of memory an arena hands out:

Java
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024);   // 32 MiB outside the heap
    block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999);
}                                                              // freed here
Kotlin
Arena.ofConfined().use { arena ->
    val block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024)              // 32 MiB outside the heap
    block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999)
}                                                              // freed here

If code uses a segment after its arena is closed, it gets an IllegalStateException with the message Already closed. In C, the same mistake reads freed memory and may silently corrupt data.

The accounting holds a surprise on JDK 25. NMT counts the confined arena's memory under Other: Other (reserved=32MB, committed=32MB) inside the arena, and 0MB after close(). But the JDK's direct buffer pool, and with it -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, counts only automatic arenas. In JDK 25's source, one line decides it: an arena counts its memory as direct memory only when the GC manages the arena's lifetime. That makes sense once you see it. An automatic arena waits for the GC, like a direct buffer, so it shares their limit; a confined arena is freed when you say so. With -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m, the demo's confined 32 MiB worked, and its automatic 32 MiB failed with Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory.

The labs compile for JDK 21, where FFM is still a preview, so this demo is a single file that runs outside Gradle on JDK 22 or later.

That's also where today's tools stop. A heap dump is one moment of the floor, NMT counts categories rather than callers, and neither one names the line of code that keeps writing the list. They tell you where to look. Reading that code is still your job.

try.title: Free 32 MiB at a closing brace (JDK 22 or later)
steps: This one runs outside Gradle and needs JDK 22 or later, ideally 25. Check with java -version. From labs/, run java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc; its commands are at the top of ArenaDemo.kt.
Predict the Other line inside the arena and after close(), then run it.
Run it again with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m in place of the NMT flag, and see which of the two arenas the limit stops.

code.title: ArenaDemo.java (JDK 22 or later)
code.html: // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. From labs/: // java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java import java.lang.foreign.Arena; import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment; import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import javax.management.ObjectName; public class ArenaDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { MemorySegment escaped; try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 1. one owner thread, closed by try-with-resources MemorySegment block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (long i = 0; i < block.byteSize() / Long.BYTES; i++) { block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100); // 4 million longs, and no objects } System.out.println("entry 1,000 holds " + block.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)); System.out.println("inside the arena: " + nativeOther()); escaped = block; } // 3. freed here, not by the GC System.out.println("after close(): " + nativeOther()); try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0); // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("reading after close() throws: " + e.getMessage()); } MemorySegment auto = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 5. freed only after the GC finds it unreachable, System.out.printf("an automatic arena: %d MiB counted as direct memory%n", // so it counts with direct buffers directBytes() >> 20); System.out.println("segment " + auto.byteSize()); } // Native Memory Tracking's "Other" row, where arena memory shows up (the same as jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary) static String nativeOther() throws Exception { String summary = (String) ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( new ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", new Object[] {new String[] {"summary", "scale=MB"}}, new String[] {String[].class.getName()}); if (!summary.contains("Total")) return "(start java with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary to see it)"; return summary.lines().filter(l -> l.contains(" Other (")).map(l -> l.replaceFirst("^-?\\s*", "")).findFirst() .orElse("Other: under 1 MB, so NMT leaves it out"); } // what the JDK counts against -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize: direct ByteBuffers and automatic arenas static long directBytes() { return ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class).stream() .filter(p -> p.getName().equals("direct")) .mapToLong(BufferPoolMXBean::getMemoryUsed).sum(); } }

alt.title: ArenaDemo.kt (JDK 22 or later)
alt.html: // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Needs the Kotlin command-line compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt -include-runtime -d memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. import java.lang.foreign.Arena import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import javax.management.ObjectName // Native Memory Tracking's "Other" row, where arena memory shows up (the same as jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary) fun nativeOther(): String { val summary = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", arrayOf<Any>(arrayOf("summary", "scale=MB")), arrayOf(Array<String>::class.java.name)) as String if ("Total" !in summary) return "(start java with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary to see it)" return summary.lines().firstOrNull { " Other (" in it }?.trim()?.removePrefix("-")?.trim() ?: "Other: under 1 MB, so NMT leaves it out" } // what the JDK counts against -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize: direct ByteBuffers and automatic arenas fun directBytes(): Long = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean::class.java) .filter { it.name == "direct" } .sumOf { it.memoryUsed } fun main(args: Array<String>) { // args unused; one main keeps every launcher happy val escaped: MemorySegment Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 1. one owner thread, closed by use {} val block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (i in 0 until block.byteSize() / Long.SIZE_BYTES) { block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100) // 4 million longs, and no objects } println("entry 1,000 holds ${block.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)}") println("inside the arena: ${nativeOther()}") escaped = block } // 3. freed here, not by the GC println("after close(): ${nativeOther()}") try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0) // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("reading after close() throws: ${e.message}") } val auto = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 5. freed only after the GC finds it unreachable, println("an automatic arena: %d MiB counted as direct memory".format(directBytes() shr 20)) // so it counts with direct buffers println("segment ${auto.byteSize()}") }

try.expect: On JDK 25: entry 1,000 holds 100000, then Other (reserved=32MB, committed=32MB) inside the arena and Other (reserved=0MB, committed=0MB) after close(), then reading after close() throws: Already closed and an automatic arena: 32 MiB counted as direct memory. With -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m the confined arena still works (the NMT lines just ask for the NMT flag), and the automatic arena fails with OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 16777216).

compare.title: A bounded LRU cache in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LruCache.java
java.html: final class LruCache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> map; LruCache(int maxEntries) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > maxEntries; } }; } synchronized V get(K key) { return map.get(key); } synchronized void put(K key, V value) { map.put(key, value); } }

kotlin.title: LruCache.kt
kotlin.html: class LruCache<K, V>(private val maxEntries: Int) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used private val map = object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>?): Boolean = size > maxEntries } @Synchronized fun get(key: K): V? = map[key] @Synchronized fun put(key: K, value: V) { map[key] = value } }

compare.note: LRU means least recently used: when the cache is full, the entry nobody has asked for the longest goes first. Both versions build on the same JDK class, and both need the lock, because LinkedHashMap isn't thread-safe and in access order even get changes the map. Java overrides removeEldestEntry in an anonymous subclass; Kotlin does it with an object : expression, and its eldest parameter is nullable because the JDK doesn't say whether it can be null. Kotlin returns V? from get, which puts the cache miss in the type. In a real service you'd often use a cache library with size limits and expiry, but the leak fix is the same idea in every form: decide a maximum, and make the structure enforce it.

worked.title: From a killed container to the line that leaks

steps.say: Picture an album exporter, a background job of the photo site that packs a user's photos into one download. Suppose it restarts with exit code 137 every two days. Start with the GC log, because it decides which half of memory to look at. Say its young pauses end near the same value day after day: the live heap is flat, so a heap dump would look healthy. Don't start there.

1. Measure the yard. Restart one instance with NMT, take a baseline once it's warm, and diff it a few hours later. Suppose only one category moved: Other, by hundreds of megabytes, with thousands more native allocations.
steps.code:
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary ... -jar album-exporter.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
# a few hours later
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB

steps.say: 1. Name the suspect. A growing Other is direct buffers or native code, and the JDK's direct buffer pool confirms it if its count and size keep climbing. Then find who allocates direct buffers for each album. Here it's a map that keeps one buffer per album and never removes them.
steps.code: // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per album, kept forever private final Map<String, ByteBuffer> albumBuffers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); ByteBuffer bufferFor(String albumId) { return albumBuffers.computeIfAbsent(albumId, id -> ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20)); }

alt.html: // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per album, kept forever private val albumBuffers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ByteBuffer>() fun bufferFor(albumId: String): ByteBuffer = albumBuffers.computeIfAbsent(albumId) { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 shl 20) }

steps.say: 1. Fix the lifetime, then add a guard. Give each album its memory for exactly as long as it's being packed, with a confined arena (JDK 22 or later), or remove the buffer from the map when the album is done. Then cap direct memory, so the next direct-buffer leak fails as an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace instead of a silent kill. The cap doesn't cover confined arenas; you close those yourself.
steps.code: void packAlbum(String albumId, Album album) { try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the album is packed MemorySegment buffer = arena.allocate(1 << 20); album.writeInto(buffer); upload(albumId, buffer); } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m

alt.html: fun packAlbum(albumId: String, album: Album) { Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the album is packed val buffer = arena.allocate(1 shl 20) album.writeInto(buffer) upload(albumId, buffer) } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m

lab.title: Find and fix the leaks in an upload cache
steps: Read UploadCache. A phone on a weak connection often sends the same upload twice, because it never heard the first answer, so the cache remembers the result for each upload id and hands it back on a retry. It also rejects a retry whose photo differs from the original.
Run the tests. Four of six fail. The two that pass check behaviour: a retry gets the same result, and a reused upload id with a different photo is rejected. Keep those passing.
Read the failing messages. Two tests count live objects with the class histogram, the same one jcmd GC.class_histogram prints: after 20,000 uploads, 20,000 results and 20,000 uploads are still alive.
Fix the first leak: bound the cache to maxEntries with an access-ordered LinkedHashMap and removeEldestEntry, and make the methods synchronized.

Run the tests again. The upload test still fails, now with about 500. Find out why each entry keeps its whole PhotoUpload, and replace it with what the retry check really needs: a SHA-256 digest of the photo. Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) makes the map access-ordered. Override removeEldestEntry to return size() > maxEntries.
MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(photo) gives 32 bytes, a fingerprint of the photo. Compare two digests with MessageDigest.isEqual.
The entry record is private, so you can change its fields freely, for example to record Entry(byte[] photoDigest, UploadResult result).
The leak tests allow 2 stray objects, because the test's own last local variables may still be reachable while it counts.

drill.title: Write the first commands from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. A program's container keeps growing. Write the commands you'd run, in order, to decide whether it's a heap leak or growth outside the heap, and to collect evidence for each case. Then write a bounded LRU map from memory.

answer.html: // 1. which half? read the floor of the young pauses in the GC log (rising = heap, flat = outside it) // 2. heap: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram (what) // jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof (who: dominator tree in MAT) // 3. outside: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB static <K, V> Map<K, V> lru(int maxEntries) { return Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > maxEntries; } }); }

alt.html: // 1. which half? read the floor of the young pauses in the GC log (rising = heap, flat = outside it) // 2. heap: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram (what) // jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof (who: dominator tree in MAT) // 3. outside: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline // jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB fun <K, V> lru(maxEntries: Int): MutableMap<K, V> = Collections.synchronizedMap(object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>?) = size > maxEntries })

recap: A Java leak is memory that stays reachable from a GC root after you're done with it: caches with no limit, ThreadLocals on pool threads, forgotten listeners, class loaders that can't unload.

A rising floor in the GC log means a heap leak. jcmd GC.class_histogram says what fills the heap; a heap dump and MAT's dominator tree say who holds it, ranked by retained size, with the path to the field.
A flat floor with a growing process means memory outside the heap. Start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, take a baseline, and read summary.diff.
Direct buffers are freed only after a GC collects their small heap objects, and their default limit is the max heap. Set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize so a leak fails loudly.

FFM arenas (final in JDK 22) give off-heap memory a lifetime: a confined arena frees it at close(). On JDK 25 only automatic arenas count against the direct-memory limit; NMT shows all of them under Other.
The limit of today's tools: a heap dump is one moment and NMT counts categories, not callers. They tell you where to look, but finding the code that keeps adding notes is still reading code.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you'd go from "the program keeps growing" to the line of code that leaks, for both kinds of leak.
explain.answer: First I'd read the GC log, because it says which half of memory is growing. If the after-values of young pauses keep rising, it's the heap. A class histogram shows which classes pile up, and a heap dump opened in MAT shows who holds them: the dominator tree ranks objects by retained size, what would be freed if they went away, and the path to a GC root names the static field, the thread or the map. If the floor is flat but the process grows, it's outside the heap. I'd restart one instance with Native Memory Tracking, take a baseline, and diff it later to see which category grows: Other points at direct buffers or native code, Thread at threads that never end, Class or Metaspace at class loaders. Then I'd fix the lifetime in code, bound caches, close arenas, and set MaxDirectMemorySize so the next direct-buffer leak fails with a stack trace.

deeper.html:
A few details make leak hunting faster.

A histogram is cheap enough to take twice. Take one, wait ten minutes under load, take another, and compare instance counts: the class whose count only goes up is your lead, even before you have a dump. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram -all skips the full GC and counts unreachable objects too, which helps when you can't afford the pause and misleads when you forget the flag.

Heap dumps are large: about the size of the live heap, here 52 MB for 44 MB of leak. GC.heap_dump -gz=1 compresses while writing. Writing a dump stops the JVM, so in a group of identical services, take it from one instance after you've stopped sending it traffic.

MAT's GC roots have kinds, and the kind is a clue. A System Class root means a static field. A Thread root, "a started, but not stopped, thread" in MAT's words, means something reachable from a live thread: its stack or its thread-locals. JNI Global means native code is holding a reference.

Class loader leaks look different from object leaks. Each reload of an application creates a new class loader with new classes. If anything from outside still references one object of an old class, for example a database driver registered in a global list, a ThreadLocal on a shared thread or a static cache in a library, the whole old class loader and every class it loaded stay in metaspace. NMT shows Class and Metaspace growing, and GC logs show collections with the cause Metadata GC Threshold. A service in production rarely reloads, but tools that reload code on every change, and long test suites, do.

Finally, jol-cli, JOL's command-line version, can estimate how a heap dump's objects would lay out under other JVM settings. For a similar 50 MB dump full of 2 KB arrays, it estimated 1.3% less with compact object headers and 3.2% more without compressed references. A heap of big arrays gains little from smaller headers, as lesson 1 predicted.
